prompt: An online furniture marketplace and its customers both use AI. Sort each system by the side of the marketplace it works for.

cards.text: A model that orders sofa search results by predicted conversion and margin
cards.explanation: Ranking search results to raise conversion and margin serves the retailer's objectives.

cards.text: A chat assistant told to find a desk under $300 that fits a 120 cm wall
cards.explanation: It represents the buyer's stated preferences and budget constraint.

cards.text: A system that picks which shoppers receive a 15 percent off coupon this week
cards.explanation: Personalizing promotions is a firm-side use aimed at conversion and lifetime value.

cards.text: An agent that compares three bookshelves across retailers and places the order
cards.explanation: Comparing prices and executing a purchase on the buyer's behalf is consumer-side AI.

cards.text: A generative model that writes 40 versions of a banner ad for different audiences
cards.explanation: Automating creative production is a firm-side use.

cards.text: A browser assistant that hides every listing without free returns, as the user asked
cards.explanation: It filters products according to the buyer's instructions.

prompt: A streaming service is deciding whom to send a retention offer. For each subscriber, name the uplift group.

cases.text: Stays if sent a free month, cancels if left alone
cases.explanation: The offer changes this subscriber's behavior, which is the only case where it pays.

cases.text: Watches every night and renews whether or not an offer arrives
cases.explanation: This subscriber stays regardless, so an offer is a wasted discount.

cases.text: Forgot about the auto-renewing plan and cancels as soon as an offer email reminds them of it
cases.explanation: Contact triggers the cancellation, so this subscriber should be left alone.

cases.text: Is moving abroad where the service is unavailable, and leaves with or without an offer
cases.explanation: This subscriber leaves regardless, so an offer changes nothing.

cases.text: Has a high churn score and stays only when the price drops for three months
cases.explanation: The intervention itself raises the chance of staying.

cases.text: Has a high churn score and leaves whether contacted or not
cases.explanation: High risk of leaving does not imply responsiveness to an offer.

prompt: An online bookstore shows a recommendation in each case. Decide which method produced it.

cases.text: Readers who bought the same four mystery novels as you also bought this thriller, so it is recommended to you
cases.explanation: The signal is the overlapping purchase histories of similar readers.

cases.text: A cookbook released this morning, with no sales yet, is recommended because its tags match cookbooks you rated highly
cases.explanation: A new item with no interactions can only be matched on its attributes, which avoids the cold-start problem.

cases.text: A first-time visitor who searched for 'space travel' sees books whose descriptions mention astronauts and rockets
cases.explanation: With no history for this visitor, the system matches item descriptions to the stated interest.

cases.text: A poetry collection is recommended because shoppers with reading histories like yours often bought it
cases.explanation: The recommendation comes from the preferences of other users with similar patterns.

cases.text: A biography is recommended because its cover image embedding resembles covers you clicked before
cases.explanation: Image embeddings are descriptive attributes of the item itself.

question_text: A grocery app always shows the five snacks with the highest past click rate in its top row. A new protein bar launched last month has almost no clicks and has never appeared there. What is the most likely problem?

options.option_text: The protein bar is clearly worse than the five snacks shown
options.option_explanation: The bar has never been shown in the top row, so the app has no evidence about how it performs there.

options.option_text: The app has too many snacks in its catalog to rank them
options.option_explanation: Catalog size is not the issue here. The issue is how the app chooses which items to display.

options.option_text: The app only exploits, so the new bar never gathers enough clicks to be shown
options.option_explanation: Correct. Pure exploitation creates a closed feedback loop: popular items keep the impressions and new items never collect the data needed to prove themselves.

options.option_text: The app should show only new items until all of them have many clicks
options.option_explanation: Showing only untested items gives up the revenue from proven winners. A bandit reserves a controlled share of impressions for testing instead.

prompt: A coffee chain's research team wants to use synthetic respondents. Sort each task by whether language-model personas are a sound tool for it.

cards.text: Checking whether the question 'How often do you buy specialty drinks?' reads ambiguously
cards.explanation: Pre-testing questionnaire wording is a valid early-stage use.

cards.text: Deciding whether a new oat-milk latte can be priced at $6.75
cards.explanation: Willingness to pay for a genuinely new product must be measured on real consumers.

cards.text: Brainstorming reasons customers might dislike a new subscription plan
cards.explanation: Generating hypotheses about possible objections is exploratory work that personas can speed up.

cards.text: Forecasting how many cups a new store will sell in its first month
cards.explanation: Demand estimation needs human data, since model answers show lower variance than real populations.

cards.text: Measuring how much a small community of competitive cyclists values a pre-ride espresso
cards.explanation: Language models under-represent niche consumer segments, so this needs real respondents.

cards.text: Drafting an interview guide before focus groups begin
cards.explanation: Accelerating survey design and qualitative exploration is a sound use.

prompt: A headphone brand is reviewing its product page. Sort each element by whether it mainly works on human shoppers or on AI shopping agents.

cards.text: A photo of a runner wearing the headphones at sunrise
cards.explanation: Lifestyle photography moves people but carries no data an agent can check.

cards.text: A specification table listing battery life as 38 hours
cards.explanation: Structured specifications let an agent filter by exact thresholds.
Psychological pricing has little effect on an agent that calculates total cost.

cards.text: An average rating of 4.5 from 3,800 reviews shown as text
cards.explanation: Aggregated review statistics are one of the cues agents parse.

cards.text: A short film about the founder's love of live music
cards.explanation: Emotional brand narratives speak to people, not to an agent screening listings.

cards.text: Warranty terms and total delivered price stated in plain text
cards.explanation: Agents read warranty terms and total delivered price directly.

question_text: A travel site tests an AI booking agent on the same eight hotels, reshuffled into a new order for each of 1,000 trials. Whichever hotel appears first is booked in 40 percent of trials. What does this show?

options.option_text: The hotels listed first are usually the best ones
options.option_explanation: The order was reshuffled each time, so the first slot held a different hotel in different trials. Merit cannot explain the pattern.

options.option_text: The agent shows primacy bias: list position, not merit, drives its choice
options.option_explanation: Correct. With identical hotels in random order, a neutral agent would book the first one about 1 time in 8. The excess is position bias.

options.option_text: The agent shows recency bias toward the end of the list
options.option_explanation: Recency bias favors the last items. Here the agent favors the first position.

options.option_text: The agent has learned the traveler's preferences over the trials
options.option_explanation: Each trial used the same hotels in a new order, so the only thing that changed was position.
